concepts.name: Monolith versus microservices
concepts.summary: Explain how a single deployable application differs from a set of small services that are deployed and scaled independently.

concepts.name: Independent deployability
concepts.summary: Understand that each service can be built, released and scaled without redeploying the others.

concepts.name: Service responsibility and size
concepts.summary: Describe a service as focused on one business capability rather than a technical layer or arbitrary line count.

concepts.name: Database per service
concepts.summary: Understand that each service owns its data and other services access it only through the service's API.

concepts.name: Synchronous service calls
concepts.summary: Recall that services can call each other over the network with request-response protocols such as REST.

concepts.name: Benefits and costs trade-off
concepts.summary: Explain the main benefits (independent scaling, team autonomy, fault isolation) and costs (network latency, operational complexity, distributed failures).

misconceptions.text: Microservices are always better than a monolith.
A service is a microservice simply because it is small in lines of code.
Several services can safely share one database as long as each uses its own tables.

concepts.name: Bounded context decomposition
concepts.summary: Apply domain-driven design to draw service boundaries around bounded contexts in a simple business domain.

concepts.name: API gateway routing
concepts.summary: Configure a gateway to route client requests to services and handle cross-cutting concerns such as authentication and rate limiting.

concepts.name: Asynchronous messaging basics
concepts.summary: Use a message broker with queues or topics so that services communicate without waiting for each other.

concepts.name: Contract-based service APIs
concepts.summary: Define and version service interfaces so that changes do not break consumers.

concepts.name: Containerised service deployment
concepts.summary: Package and run each service as its own container with its own configuration and dependencies.

concepts.name: Service discovery
concepts.summary: Use a registry or platform DNS so that services find each other when instances change address.

concepts.name: Distributed logging and tracing
concepts.summary: Understand how correlation IDs and centralised logs let you follow a request across services.

misconceptions.text: Services should be split by technical layer, such as one for the UI, one for business logic and one for data.
The API gateway is the place to put all business logic shared between services.
Asynchronous messaging is just a faster version of synchronous calls.

concepts.name: Context mapping and ownership
concepts.summary: Analyse relationships between contexts and teams, including upstream/downstream dependencies and anti-corruption layers, to refine boundaries.

concepts.name: REST versus gRPC trade-offs
concepts.summary: Compare REST, gRPC and messaging for a given interaction in terms of coupling, performance, typing and client needs.

concepts.name: Eventual consistency handling
concepts.summary: Analyse where data across services may be temporarily stale and design workflows and user experience to tolerate it.

concepts.name: Circuit breaker and timeouts
concepts.summary: Apply timeouts, retries with backoff and circuit breakers to stop failures from cascading between services.

concepts.name: Idempotent message handling
concepts.summary: Analyse delivery guarantees and make consumers idempotent so that duplicates and redelivery do not corrupt state.

concepts.name: Saga pattern
concepts.summary: Implement multi-service business transactions as a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, using choreography or orchestration.

concepts.name: Event-driven data propagation
concepts.summary: Analyse how services publish domain events and maintain local read copies of data owned by others.

misconceptions.text: Retrying failed calls always improves reliability.
A saga gives the same isolation and atomicity guarantees as a database transaction.
A message broker guarantees each message is delivered exactly once, so consumers need no duplicate handling.

concepts.name: Strangler fig migration
concepts.summary: Evaluate and sequence the incremental extraction of capabilities from a monolith behind a routing facade, deciding what to extract first.

concepts.name: Data separation during migration
concepts.summary: Analyse approaches such as shared-schema stages, synchronisation and change data capture for pulling data out of a monolith database.

concepts.name: Transactional outbox pattern
concepts.summary: Analyse how writing events to an outbox in the same local transaction avoids losing or inventing events when updating state and publishing.

concepts.name: CQRS and read models
concepts.summary: Evaluate when separate read models or API composition are justified for queries spanning multiple services.

concepts.name: Observability and SLO design
concepts.summary: Analyse metrics, traces and logs to find bottlenecks and failure sources, and set service-level objectives.

concepts.name: Consumer-driven contract testing
concepts.summary: Evaluate a testing strategy that balances unit, contract, integration and end-to-end tests across services.

concepts.name: Service-to-service security
concepts.summary: Analyse how authentication, authorisation and token propagation work between services behind a gateway.

misconceptions.text: Migrating to microservices should start with a full rewrite of the monolith.
Publishing an event right after committing to the database is reliable enough without an outbox.
End-to-end tests alone are sufficient to verify that services work together.

concepts.name: Architecture fitness evaluation
concepts.summary: Judge whether microservices, a modular monolith or a hybrid best fits an organisation's scale, team structure and domain volatility.

concepts.name: Boundary evolution and refactoring
concepts.summary: Critique existing boundaries and decide when to merge, split or re-draw services to remove coupling and chatty communication.

concepts.name: Resilience and chaos strategy
concepts.summary: Design a resilience programme with graceful degradation, load shedding and failure-injection experiments across a service landscape.

concepts.name: Consistency model design
concepts.summary: Design how business invariants are enforced across services, choosing between sagas, reservation patterns, and relaxed or redefined rules.

concepts.name: Platform and governance design
concepts.summary: Create shared platform capabilities and governance, such as templates, standards and deployment pipelines, that keep many teams autonomous yet consistent.

concepts.name: Event schema evolution strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate compatibility rules, schema registries and versioning approaches so that producers and consumers evolve independently.

concepts.name: Cost and organisational impact
concepts.summary: Evaluate the operational cost and team-topology effects of a service architecture, including Conway's law and cognitive load.

misconceptions.text: If services are deployed separately, the architecture is automatically loosely coupled.
Every cross-service business rule must be enforced with strong consistency to be correct.
Team structure has little effect on service architecture, which is purely a technical choice.
